provenance.other: “blood crieth unto me from the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 4:10. The nearest relatives are Job 16:18 ('let my cry have no place') and Revelation 6:10, neither of which has blood crying from the ground.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the Book of Mormon's sentence acquires a genealogy it does not state. Genesis 4:10 is Abel's blood; Luke 11:50-51 makes Abel's blood the head of a series — 'the blood of all the prophets … from the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias' — required of the generation that killed them. 2 Nephi 26:3 does exactly what Luke does: it takes killed prophets and killed saints and has their blood cry from the ground for a coming judgment. The verse is Genesis' image put to Luke's use, and neither text is named.

26:3.note: 'Wherefore the cry of the blood of the saints shall ascend up to God from the ground, against them.' Ground, blood, and a cry that reaches God are Genesis 4:10's three elements in Genesis' order, with the martyrs of the church substituted for Abel. The composite is not decorative: 26:3's charge is that they 'cast out the prophets, and the saints, and stone them, and slay them', which is the charge of Matthew 23:35-37 and Luke 11:47-51, the two New Testament passages that already read Abel's blood as the first of the prophets'. Skousen's threshold is not met and this is not one of his 36.
26:3.text: And he said, What hast thou done? the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground.

provenance.other: The machine's longest run in this chapter, thirteen words, and “the day that cometh shall burn them up” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 4:1. Malachi reads 'all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts'; 2 Nephi 26:4 reads 'all they that are proud, and that do wickedly, the day that cometh shall burn them up saith the Lord of Hosts, for they shall be as stubble'.
provenance.significance: Malachi 4 is the last chapter of the Old Testament and is quoted entire later in this corpus, at 3 Nephi 25, from the mouth of the risen Christ. Its two halves are split here across 2 Nephi 26: v. 1's burning of the proud at 26:4 and 26:6, v. 2's Sun of righteousness with healing in his wings at 25:13 and 26:9. So the chapter Christ will one day deliver whole is already dismantled and redistributed in Nephi's exposition six hundred years earlier, and the seam between the burning and the healing has become the seam between the wicked and the righteous at 26:8.

26:4.note: An unmarked quotation, and the clearest in the chapter. Nephi reorders Malachi's clauses — the stubble moves from before the burning to after it, and 'saith the Lord of Hosts' stays fixed in the middle where Malachi has it — but every content word is Malachi's and the whole is well above any verbal threshold. Hardy cross-references Malachi 4:1 here.
26:4.text: For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

provenance.other: “grind him to powder” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 21:44 and Luke 20:18, which are the same saying in the two gospels. The image exists in English scripture only there.
provenance.significance: In both gospels the saying belongs to the parable of the wicked husbandmen who killed the householder's servants and then his son, and it is the stone that grinds — the rejected stone become head of the corner. 2 Nephi 26:5 is about 'they that kill the prophets, and the saints', which is the parable's subject, and the agent of the grinding here is a falling building: 'buildings shall fall upon them, and crush them to pieces, and grind them to powder'. The gospel's falling stone has become a falling building, and the sin it punishes is the parable's.

26:5.note: The verse assembles four destructions and the last of them is a gospel phrase used with its own occasion attached. Note the direction of the metaphor: Christ's saying is about what happens to whoever falls on the stone or has it fall on him, and Nephi keeps the falling and the grinding while losing the stone.
26:5.text: And whosoever shall fall on this stone shall be broken: but on whomsoever it shall fall, it will grind him to powder.

provenance.other: The KJV assigns the two verbs differently in its two versions of this cry. Hosea 10:8: 'they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.' Luke 23:30 reverses them: 'to the mountains, Fall on us; and to the hills, Cover us.' Revelation 6:16 has 'mountains and rocks, Fall on us'. “to the mountains, Cover us” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 10:8.
provenance.significance: Nephi writes 'and mountains shall cover them', which is Hosea's pairing and not Luke's or Revelation's. The distinction is worth having because Luke 23:30 is the version a nineteenth-century reader would know best — it is Christ's word to the daughters of Jerusalem on the way to the cross — and the Book of Mormon's verb goes the other way. Where the pairing is a coin-flip, the coin landing on the Old Testament side is a small piece of evidence about which text was in view.

26:5.note: Three words, so the row is graded moderate and rests entirely on the verb assignment. Recorded because the assignment is testable and comes out cleanly: mountains cover in Hosea and in Nephi, mountains fall in Luke and Revelation. The rest of the verse's destructions are separately sourced (Matthew 21:44 above) or generic; 'the depths of the earth shall swallow them up' recalls Korah at Numbers 16:32 but shares only the swallowing.
26:5.whyNot: 'Mountains shall cover them' is short, and an independent writer imagining apocalyptic destruction has a limited stock of verbs. The evidence is a preference between two KJV forms, not a borrowing that could only have one home.
26:5.text: The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

provenance.other: “anger of the LORD kindled” — the participial form without the auxiliary — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:25. The far commoner narrative formula, 'the anger of the LORD was kindled', occurs in eleven. Isaiah 5:24 supplies the stubble consumed by fire, and this book transcribes both verses at 2 Nephi 15:24-25.
provenance.significance: Two chapters of scripture are fused in one sentence, and this catalogue can show that the book already contains both. Malachi 4:1 gives the stubble and the consuming day; Isaiah 5:24-25 gives the fire that devours the stubble and the kindled anger. Nephi's clause — 'for the fire of the anger of the Lord shall be kindled against them, and they shall be as stubble, and the day that cometh shall consume them' — runs the two together in a single breath, and the joint is the word 'stubble', which both sources have. That is a compositional method, not an echo.

26:6.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 5:24-25 and Malachi 4:1 together at this verse, which is exactly right, and the catalogue records both: Malachi as a recurrence of the row at 26:4, Isaiah here. Mediation is OT-via-earlier-BoM because Isaiah 5 is transcribed in this same book eleven chapters earlier; the transcription at 2 Nephi 15:25 preserves the KJV's 'Therefore is the anger of the Lord kindled', and 26:6 recasts it as a future.
26:6.text: Therefore is the anger of the LORD kindled against his people, and he hath stretched forth his hand against them, and hath smitten them: and the hills did tremble, and their carcases were torn in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still.

provenance.other: “thunderings, and lightnings” in that order occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 8:5, 'there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake'. Revelation 11:19 and 16:18 have the same catalogue with the terms in a different order; Exodus 19:16 has 'thunders and lightnings' without the -ing forms.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon's list is Revelation's list with the voices removed: thunderings, lightnings, earthquakes, and then 'all manner of destructions'. What is being borrowed is a genre marker — the plural verbal nouns are how the King James Apocalypse says that the world is being unmade — and Nephi attaches it to a Malachi judgment, so the Old Testament day of burning arrives with the New Testament's stage machinery.

26:6.note: The order of the three terms is the evidence; the terms themselves are the common stock of apocalyptic. Graded moderate for that reason. Note that the 1830 'thunderings' preserves the KJV's form exactly.
26:6.text: And the angel took the censer, and filled it with fire of the altar, and cast it into the earth: and there were voices, and thunderings, and lightnings, and an earthquake.

provenance.other: “just and true are thy ways” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 15:3. Deuteronomy 32:4 has 'all his ways are judgment' and Psalm 145:17 'the LORD is righteous in all his ways'; neither supplies the predicate adjective with the second person.
provenance.significance: This is the verse 1 Nephi opened on. Lehi's praise at 1 Nephi 1:14 borrows six words from Revelation 15:3 — 'Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty' — and Revelation identifies those words as 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Nephi now takes the second half of the same sentence, and takes it at the point of greatest strain: he has just seen the destruction of his own people and says 'I must cry unto my God, thy ways are just'. The father sang the song of Moses in triumph at the beginning of the record; the son quotes its next clause as a submission. Recovering Revelation 15:3 supplies both halves of that arc, and neither Nephi nor Lehi names it.

26:7.note: Three words, inverted from Revelation's order ('just and true are thy ways' → 'thy ways are just') and stripped of 'true'. The row is written rather than excluded as a repeat because 1 Nephi and 2 Nephi are different books (ADJUDICATING §4) and because the use is not the same use: 1 Nephi 1:14 is doxology, 2 Nephi 26:7 is theodicy. The argument that Revelation 15:3 is the source was made at 1 Nephi 1:14 and is not restated here.
26:7.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: The KJV reads 'the Sun of righteousness shall … arise with healing in his wings'. The 1830 first edition reads 'the Son of righteousness shall appear unto them; and he shall heal them'. The homophone is not a modern printing error: 'Son' stands in the first edition and in the current text alike.
provenance.significance: CONVENTIONS §8 asks whether an 1830 reading bears on the judgment, and here the reading is the judgment. Malachi's image is astronomical — a winged sun-disc rising — and the Book of Mormon converts it to a title, Son of righteousness, and unpacks the wings into a verb: 'he shall heal them'. Nine verses earlier, at 25:13, the same chapter of Malachi was quoted with the wings intact and applied to the resurrection. So within a dozen verses the catalogue can watch one KJV verse used twice, once as an image kept whole and once as an image resolved into the doctrine it was taken to contain. The homophone is available only in English, which makes this among the strongest kjvSpecific claims in the book: no Hebrew reader has the option of hearing shemesh as a son.

26:9.note: Hardy cross-references Malachi 4:2 here and the reference is exact. What the catalogue adds is the pairing with 25:13: 'healing in his wings' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 4:2, and this book uses that verse twice in two chapters by two different methods. The 'Son'/'Sun' reading has a long history of comment in Latter-day Saint sources and is not this catalogue's discovery; it is recorded here for what it shows about the route, which is a route through English.
26:9.text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.

provenance.other: “third and fourth generation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Exodus 20:5, Numbers 14:18 and Deuteronomy 5:9, and in all three it is the reach of visited iniquity: 'visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation'.
provenance.significance: Nephi's clause runs 'until three generations shall have passed away, and many of the fourth generation shall have passed away in righteousness'. The biblical formula measures how far a sin travels down a family; the Book of Mormon uses the same span to measure how long a righteousness lasts, and then 26:10 lets the destruction fall exactly where the formula said it would. The inversion is not casual — twenty-three verses later, at 26:32, Nephi rehearses the Decalogue from the chapter this formula belongs to.

26:9.note: An allusion at the level of a measure rather than a phrase, which is why it is graded moderate and typed as an echo. It is recorded because the same chapter supplies the Decalogue at 26:32, so Exodus 20 is demonstrably in view in this chapter, and because a positive use of a formula that is negative everywhere in the KJV is the kind of reversal worth catching. The machine proposed 2 Kings 10:30's promise to Jehu instead, which shares more words and none of the sense; that candidate is in the register.
26:9.text: Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;

provenance.other: “sold yourselves for nought” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 52:3. Note that Isaiah 52:3 falls just outside this book's transcribed Isaiah: 2 Nephi 7-8 carry Isaiah 50 and 51:1-52:2 and stop one verse short, so unlike almost every other Isaiah borrowing in 2 Nephi 25-30 this one has no transcription in the book to point back to.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:3 completes as 'and ye shall be redeemed without money' — the sale is worthless and so is the ransom, and the whole point is that the redemption costs nothing. Nephi takes the first half and drops the second: his people 'sell themselves for nought' and what follows is not redemption but 'they shall reap destruction … therefore they must go down to hell'. The suppressed half is the mercy, and it returns fifteen verses later at 26:25, where Isaiah 55:1's 'without money and without price' is quoted outright. Isaiah's two halves are separated by fifteen verses of Nephi's argument.

26:10.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 52:3 here. The Book of Mormon shifts person — 'ye have sold yourselves' to 'they sell themselves' — and tense, which is what one expects of exposition rather than transcription. The 1830 has the ungrammatical 'because they yieldeth unto the Devil' in the same sentence, retained in 1920.
26:10.text: For thus saith the LORD, Ye have sold yourselves for nought; and ye shall be redeemed without money.

provenance.other: “rather than light” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:19: 'men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil'.
provenance.significance: John 3:19 is the New Testament's definition of condemnation as a preference, and the Book of Mormon's verse is built on exactly that: not that men are overtaken by darkness but that they 'choose works of darkness rather than light'. The one substitution — 'choose' for 'loved' — hardens the verse into an act of will, which is the doctrine 2 Nephi 2 spent a chapter establishing. And the chapter answers itself at 26:23: 'the Lord God worketh not in darkness'.

26:10.note: Three words, a KJV singleton, and the whole comparative structure of John's sentence. 'Works of darkness' is Pauline (Romans 13:12, Ephesians 5:11) and was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 25:2; here it is fused with John's comparative, so the clause has two New Testament parents. The n-gram stream saw neither, because both agreements are split across intervening words.
26:10.text: And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world, and men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil.

provenance.other: “my spirit shall not always strive with man” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 6:3. The Book of Mormon reproduces it with the possessive turned to a genitive — 'the spirit of the Lord will not always strive with man' — and then repeats the verb twice more in the next clause.
provenance.significance: Genesis 6:3 is the sentence God speaks immediately before the flood: the withdrawal of the striving spirit is the announcement of universal destruction. Nephi quotes it and then supplies the inference Genesis leaves to the narrative — 'and when the spirit ceaseth to strive with man, then cometh speedy destruction'. The flood is not mentioned. It does not need to be: the reader who knows where the sentence comes from knows what follows it, and Nephi's 'speedy destruction' is the deluge's speed transferred to his own people. This is metalepsis in Hays's sense, and it is the chapter's best instance.

26:11.note: Eight words from a KJV singleton, and the strongest borrowing in the chapter after Malachi 4:1. Hardy does not cross-reference it. The change from 'my spirit' to 'the spirit of the Lord' is required by the shift from divine speech to prophetic exposition, and the added gloss in the second clause shows the writer working out the consequence of the verse rather than merely echoing it.
26:11.text: And the LORD said, My spirit shall not always strive with man, for that he also is flesh: yet his days shall be an hundred and twenty years.

provenance.other: “very Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 9:22 and John 7:26. Acts 9:22 is Saul at Damascus 'confounding the Jews … proving that this is very Christ'; John 7:26 is the crowd asking whether the rulers know 'that this is the very Christ'.
provenance.significance: Nephi's sentence is 'as I spake concerning the convincing of the Jews, that Jesus is the very Christ'. Acts 9:22 is the New Testament's one description of exactly that activity — a man convincing Jews that Jesus is very Christ — and its verb, 'confounded … proving', is the work Nephi has assigned to his own record at 25:18 ('for the purpose of convincing them of the true Messiah'). The unusual adjective and the unusual task arrive together.

26:12.note: 'Very' as an adjective meaning 'true, real' is archaic English and its collocation with Christ is confined to two verses; that is what makes two words worth a row. Graded moderate because the phrase is short and because the next clause drops it — 'that the Gentiles be convinced also, that Jesus is the Christ, the Eternal God' — which suggests the writer is not holding a source open in front of him.
26:12.text: But Saul increased the more in strength, and confounded the Jews which dwelt at Damascus, proving that this is very Christ.

provenance.other: “every nation, and kindred, and tongue” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:6. The fourfold formula appears elsewhere in Revelation with 'people' first or 'kindreds' plural (5:9, 7:9, 11:9, 13:7); only 14:6 has this order with 'every' governing.
provenance.significance: Revelation 14:6's four nouns belong to the angel with the everlasting gospel to preach to them that dwell on the earth. Nephi's sentence is about Christ manifesting himself 'unto every nation, kindred, tongue, and people, working mighty miracles, signs and wonders' — the same universality and the same commission, with Christ himself in the angel's place. The verse would become the Latter-day Saint proof-text for the restoration; here it is doing the plainer work of saying that the gospel has no ethnic boundary, which is 26:33's conclusion.

26:13.note: A four-term list in a KJV singleton's order, with the conjunctions dropped as the Book of Mormon habitually drops them. 'Signs and wonders' in the same clause occurs in thirteen KJV verses and cannot be sourced; it is not counted toward this row.
26:13.text: And I saw another angel fly in the midst of heaven, having the everlasting gospel to preach unto them that dwell on the earth, and to every nation, and kindred, and tongue, and people,

provenance.other: Isaiah 29:3 reads 'And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.' 2 Nephi 26:15 reads 'the Lord God shall have camped against them round about, and shall have laid siege against them with a mount, and raised forts against them'. Every content word is Isaiah's; only person and tense change. “lay siege against thee with a mount” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:3.
provenance.significance: This is the structural fact that governs 2 Nephi 26 and 27 together, and it is worth stating once. Isaiah 29 enters the Book of Mormon twice and in two pieces. Verses 3-5 — the siege, the voice from the dust, the chaff — are used here at 26:15-18 and applied to the destruction of Nephi's own seed. Verses 6-24 are expanded at 2 Nephi 27 and applied to the last days and the coming forth of a book. Verses 1-2, the only part naming Ariel and 'the city where David dwelt', are used nowhere: the one section that ties the oracle to Jerusalem is the section that is dropped. So the chapter is not simply quoted, it is dismembered along a line that removes its geography and distributes its two halves to two different peoples and two different centuries.

26:15.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:3-5 at 26:14, one verse before the wording begins; CONVENTIONS §6a puts the link where the wording is and the register at 26:14 sends the reader here. Three clauses reproduced in Isaiah's order with the subject changed from God speaking in the first person to God reported in the third, which is what an expositor does and a transcriber does not.
26:15.text: And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee.

provenance.other: “whisper out of the dust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:4, and the machine's rarity score for this pairing, 10.02 on a nine-word run, is the second highest in the chapter. Isaiah's four elements all appear: speaking out of the ground, speech low out of the dust, a voice as of one that hath a familiar spirit, and a whisper out of the dust.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:4 is a threat: the besieged city is brought so low that its voice comes from underground like a necromancer's ghost, and the simile is contemptuous — a familiar spirit is what Leviticus 20:27 says to stone a person for consulting. The Book of Mormon reverses the valuation entirely. The voice from the dust is its own voice, the record of a destroyed people speaking to a later one, and 'the Lord God will give unto him power, that he may whisper concerning them' turns the ghost into an authorised messenger. This is the verse the book uses to describe itself — Moroni will return to it, and 2 Nephi 33:13 speaks 'as the voice of one crying from the dust' — so an oracle of humiliation has been made the Book of Mormon's account of its own mode of existence.
provenance.alternative: None; the wording has no other KJV home.

26:16.note: The chapter's densest borrowing after Malachi 4:1, and its most consequential. Isaiah's second person becomes third and the passive becomes an act of divine enabling, but the four clauses stand in Isaiah's order. Note the added agent: Isaiah has no one giving power to whisper. Hardy's cross-reference to Isaiah 29:4 is keyed to 2 Nephi 27:13, where the wording is only a paraphrase ('speak as if it were from the dead'); the verbal link belongs here.
26:16.text: And thou shalt be brought down, and shalt speak out of the ground, and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be, as of one that hath a familiar spirit, out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust.

provenance.other: “chaff that passeth away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:5, and “at an instant” in exactly two, Isaiah 29:5 and 30:13. The Book of Mormon has both, in Isaiah's order, with 'suddenly' following: 'It shall be at an instant, suddenly.'
provenance.significance: Isaiah 29:5's first half — 'the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust' — is dropped, and the second half kept. That is consistent with what 26:15-18 is doing to the whole oracle: the strangers besieging a city have no place in a prophecy about a people destroying itself, so the besiegers go and the suddenness stays. The Book of Mormon also reads 'their terrible ones' where the KJV has 'the terrible ones', which attaches the multitude to the destroyed people rather than to their attackers, completing the transfer.

26:18.note: Two KJV rarities in one clause, one of them a singleton, and the second sentence — 'Yea, thus saith the Lord God: It shall be at an instant, suddenly' — reproduces Isaiah's closing words with a messenger formula prefixed. The pronoun change from 'the' to 'their' is the interpretive move and it is worth recording as such.
26:18.text: Moreover the multitude of thy strangers shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the terrible ones shall be as chaff that passeth away: yea, it shall be at an instant suddenly.

provenance.other: “grind the faces of the poor” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 3:15, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 13:15. The Book of Mormon's exposition alters the preposition — 'grind upon the face of the poor' — and the singular 'face'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 3:15 is addressed to 'the ancients of his people, and the princes thereof': the grinders are the rulers of Judah. Nephi transfers the charge to Gentile churchmen who 'preach up unto themselves, their own wisdom, and their own learning, that they may get gain'. The oracle against a native ruling class is redirected at a foreign religious one, and the mechanism of the oppression changes from judicial to commercial.

26:20.note: One of three Isaiah phrases fused in this verse — with Isaiah 2:11's lofty looks and Isaiah 8:14's stone of stumbling, both catalogued below — and all three come from chapters this book has already transcribed. Hardy cross-references all three at this verse and the reference is exact in each case. The catalogue splits them into separate rows because they come from three different oracles and are doing three different things.
26:20.text: What mean ye that ye beat my people to pieces, and grind the faces of the poor? saith the Lord GOD of hosts.

provenance.other: “stone of stumbling” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 8:14 and 1 Peter 2:8, which quotes it. This book transcribes Isaiah 8:14 at 2 Nephi 18:14.
provenance.significance: In Isaiah the stone of stumbling is the Lord of hosts himself, a sanctuary to some and a snare to others; in Romans 9:32 and 1 Peter 2:8 it is Christ, and men stumble at the word. Nephi's Gentiles 'have stumbled, because of the greatness of their stumbling block' — and the stumbling block turns out to be their own churches, 'that they have built up many Churches'. The Christological stone has been replaced by the institutions built in its name, which is a sharper reading of Isaiah than either Paul's or Peter's and is made out of their vocabulary.

26:20.note: 'Stumbling block' rather than 'stone of stumbling' is the Book of Mormon's form, and it is a KJV phrase in its own right (Leviticus 19:14, Romans 14:13 and elsewhere), so the row rests on the collocation with 'stumbled' and on Hardy's grouping of this verse with Isaiah 8:14-15. Mediation is set to OT-via-earlier-BoM: the transcription at 2 Nephi 18:14 is in this book and is the nearer model, and the New Testament reapplications are recorded as composite because Nephi's use is Christological in the way theirs are and Isaiah's is not.
26:20.text: And he shall be for a sanctuary; but for a stone of stumbling and for a rock of offence to both the houses of Israel, for a gin and for a snare to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “lofty looks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 2:11, and this book transcribes it at 2 Nephi 12:11. Isaiah 2:12 supplies 'every one that is proud and lofty, and upon every one that is lifted up'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 2:11-12 is the day of the Lord against everything high, and its refrain is that the lofty are brought low. Nephi's 'the Gentiles are lifted up in the pride of their eyes' compresses Isaiah's two verses into one clause — the lifting up from v. 12, the eyes from v. 11's lofty looks — and the day of the Lord that follows in Isaiah has already been announced in this chapter at 26:4-6.

26:20.note: Graded moderate: 'lifted up in the pride of' is not a KJV string, and the case is that the two ideas Isaiah 2:11-12 pairs are the two Nephi pairs. Hardy cross-references Isaiah 2:12-14 here, which is right and slightly wide; v. 11 supplies the eyes.
26:20.text: The lofty looks of man shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down, and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.

provenance.other: “get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13: 'ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain'.
provenance.significance: James's traders are rebuked not for trading but for presuming on a future they do not own — 'ye know not what shall be on the morrow' — and the phrase in the KJV belongs to them alone. The Book of Mormon makes it the motive of priestcraft. It uses the phrase three times in two chapters: here of churchmen who preach their own learning, at 26:29 in the definition of priestcraft itself, and at 27:16 of the learned man who asks for the sealed book 'because of the glory of the world, and to get gain'. A commercial idiom with one biblical home has become this section's standing term for religion practised for money.

26:20.note: Two words, and they carry a row because the KJV has them once and the Book of Mormon builds a doctrine on them. The link is placed at the first of the three occurrences and the other two are recorded as recurrences (ADJUDICATING §4). Graded moderate because 'get gain' is ordinary enough English that a nineteenth-century writer might reach it without James.
26:20.text: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:

provenance.other: “cords of vanity” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 5:18 — 'Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope' — transcribed in this book at 2 Nephi 15:18. The Book of Mormon shares only the noun: 'a flaxen cord', 'his strong cords'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's woe is on people who haul their own sin about like a cart; the cords are theirs and the pulling is theirs. Nephi reverses the agency completely — the devil 'leadeth them by the neck with a flaxen cord, until he bindeth them with his strong cords forever' — so the rope that was a figure for self-inflicted guilt becomes a leash held by someone else, and the woe becomes a captivity. The image also acquires a progression Isaiah has no room for: a flaxen cord first, strong cords afterwards.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 5:22, 'he shall be holden with the cords of his sins', is nearer to Isaiah's sense and further from Nephi's wording; Hosea 11:4's 'cords of a man' and 'bands of love' are the KJV's other leading-cords.

26:22.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 5:18 here, and this is a case where his row is worth having and worth qualifying. The verbal contact is one common noun; what justifies the row is that Isaiah 5 is transcribed in this same book, that Nephi has already drawn on Isaiah 5:24-25 at 26:6, and that the image of iniquity drawn with cords has no other biblical home. Graded moderate, and typed conceptual rather than verbal, because the wording is not reproduced and the sense is inverted.
26:22.text: Woe unto them that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart rope:

provenance.other: “draw all men unto me” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:32: 'And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.' “lay down my life” occurs in three, John 10:15, 10:17 and 13:37.
provenance.significance: John 12:32's drawing is conditional on the lifting up, and John 12:33 glosses the lifting up as the manner of his death. The Book of Mormon states the same causal chain without the metaphor: 'he loveth the world, even that he layeth down his own life, that he may draw all men unto him'. The crucifixion has been named rather than figured, and John's 'if I be lifted up' has become a plain purpose clause. That is a decision about how to read John 12:32, and the verse makes it silently.

26:24.note: A Johannine sentence assembled from three of John's own: 'he loveth the world' from 3:16, 'layeth down his own life' from 10:17, 'draw all men unto him' from 12:32, with the last a KJV singleton. The argument the sentence is making — that God does nothing except for the benefit of the world — is the chapter's, not John's.
26:24.text: And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.

provenance.other: “without money and without price” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 55:1, which reads 'come, buy wine and milk without money and without price'. The Book of Mormon reads 'buy milk and honey, without money, and without price'.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. Isaiah's pair is wine and milk; the Book of Mormon's is milk and honey, which is the KJV's standing formula for the land of promise — 'a land flowing with milk and honey', some twenty times from Exodus 3:8 onward. So the invitation to buy without money is answered not with Isaiah's drink but with the promised land itself, offered free. Whether the change is deliberate or a memory sliding from one fixed phrase to another, it converts an invitation to a meal into an invitation to an inheritance, which is what 2 Nephi has been promising since chapter 1. Note also that this verse retrieves the half of Isaiah 52:3 that 26:10 suppressed: 'ye shall be redeemed without money'.

26:25.note: Hardy cross-references Isaiah 55:1 here and the reference is exact. Two further sources are fused into the same sentence: 'Come unto me all' is Matthew 11:28's opening and 'all ye ends of the earth' answers Isaiah 45:22's 'Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth'. The rhetorical frame — 'doth he cry unto any, saying, Depart from me? … nay; but he saith, Come unto me' — sets Matthew 7:23's dismissal against Matthew 11:28's invitation, which is a use of the gospels against each other rather than a borrowing from either. Matthew 11 has now supplied this section three times (25:18, 25:28, here).
26:25.text: Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.

provenance.other: “have not charity” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 13:1, 2 and 3, the refrain of the chapter. 'Charity' as the KJV's rendering of ἀγάπη is itself a version-specific choice: Geneva has 'love' at 1 Corinthians 13 and modern versions almost all read 'love'.
provenance.significance: Paul's refrain is that gifts without charity leave the possessor as nothing — 'I am nothing'. Nephi turns the first person into the third and makes it a condition of a commandment: 'the Lord God hath given a commandment, that all men should have charity, which charity is love. And except they should have charity, they were nothing.' Paul does not command charity in 1 Corinthians 13; he measures the gifts against it. The Book of Mormon converts a measure into a law, and then applies the law to a labour dispute — 'they would not suffer the laborer in Zion to perish'.

26:30.note: The gloss 'which charity is love' is the interesting half of the row. It is an explanation the KJV needs and the Greek does not, and it is the sort of thing a nineteenth-century reader of the King James Bible would supply for a word whose ordinary English sense had drifted to almsgiving — which is, as it happens, exactly the sense the surrounding verses about the labourer in Zion are about to require. The dependence on 1 Corinthians 13 is not in doubt; what is worth recording is that the verse translates its source for its reader.
26:30.text: And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.

provenance.other: Nephi's list runs: not murder, not lie, not steal, not take the name of the Lord their God in vain, not envy, not have malice, not contend, not commit whoredoms. Four are Decalogue commandments in the KJV's own wording, and 'take the name of the LORD thy God in vain' is Exodus 20:7 almost verbatim with the pronoun changed. “take the name of the LORD thy God in vain” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 20:7 and its Deuteronomy 5:11 double, so the Decalogue's two recensions cannot be distinguished here.
provenance.significance: The order is the finding. The Decalogue's sequence is name, sabbath, parents, murder, adultery, theft, false witness, coveting; Nephi's is murder, lying, theft, the name, envy, malice, contention, whoredoms. The commandment against taking the name in vain has fallen from third to fourth, the sabbath and the honouring of parents are absent, and four items with no Decalogue equivalent — envy, malice, contention, whoredoms — have been appended. What emerges is not the Decalogue but a vice-list of the sort the New Testament epistles produce (Galatians 5:19-21, Colossians 3:8), built out of the Decalogue's raw material and finished with the sins the preceding verses have been describing: envy and strife at 26:21, priestcraft and gain at 26:29.

26:32.note: Hardy cross-references Exodus 20:7-17 here, which is the right range, and the interest of the row is in what the range does not cover. This is also where 26:9's allusion to Exodus 20:5's 'third and fourth generation' pays off: the same chapter of Exodus supplies the measure of the Nephite reprieve and the terms of the law they break.
26:32.text: Thou shalt not take the name of the LORD thy God in vain; for the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh his name in vain.

provenance.other: “bond nor free” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Galatians 3:28 and Colossians 3:11. Only Galatians 3:28 has the three pairs together and in this order — Jew/Greek, bond/free, male/female — and Nephi's list keeps two of them in Galatians' sequence and closes on the third: 'bond and free, male and female … both Jew and Gentile'.
provenance.significance: Galatians 3:28's point is that the distinctions are abolished in Christ; Nephi's is that they are irrelevant to invitation — 'he denieth none that come unto him'. The added pair is the one Paul does not have: 'black and white'. That is not a biblical antithesis at all, and its insertion at the head of Paul's list is the most consequential single word-choice in the chapter, since 2 Nephi 5:21 has already made skin colour a mark of curse. The catalogue records the borrowing and notes that the added term sits uneasily with the source's logic and with the book's own earlier use of it.
provenance.alternative: Colossians 3:11 shares 'bond nor free' and adds Barbarian and Scythian, but lacks male and female.

26:33.note: The chapter's last sentence and its best-known one. Three Pauline pairs, one interpolated pair, and a closing 'both Jew and Gentile' that returns to the head of Galatians' list — so the verse both opens and closes on Paul's first antithesis. 'He inviteth them all to come unto him' is Matthew 11:28's verb again and 'he denieth none that come unto him' answers John 6:37, which was adjudicated at 2 Nephi 25:29; both are recorded as composite rather than given their own rows.
26:33.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
